title: The Park Job
text:
She was waiting in the alley when he came down, hood up against a thin rain, her field kit at her feet and the big static wand slung across her back, a spool of splice line in one hand and a look of barely civilized excitement on her face.

"Before you say anything," she said — which was how she opened every negotiation she'd already won — "the contract says the engineer may attend. That's me. I'm the engineer. It said so in writing. I'm having the line framed."

"It's a job, not a gala."

"It's the first thing your spooky perfect client has asked for in eleven years of paper, and it said BRING THE SWORD, which means hardware, which means the engineer attends with the big wand." She shouldered the kit. "Also I checked the site. The park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> sits on the old <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity> trunk, and the carousel's been dead since before either of us could legally work. Whatever it wants down there, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity> — it's not a pony ride."

He looked at her a second longer than the joke needed, then took the spool from her hand so she'd have one free.

He turned the spool over in his palm as he did it, and that was when the alley light caught the label. Not the deep-blue seal he'd checked out of the shop that morning. A stripped core — the cheap gray of comm-grade filament, no shielding rating on it at all.

"This isn't the line I signed for," he said.

"It's the line that was in the locker." She was already reaching for it, already fitting the answer together on her face and not liking the shape of it. "I pulled it myself. The blue spools were—" She stopped. "The blue spools were logged out. All four. This morning. Before I got there."

"Logged out to who?"

"Doesn't say." Her excitement had gone somewhere colder. "Which it always says. That's the whole point of the log."

So: no shielded splice line, a client who'd waited eleven years to name the hour, and someone ahead of them who'd already emptied the locker of the only cable that would survive whatever was live on the <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity> trunk. He weighed the useless gray spool and felt the job change under his hands from a gala she'd talked her way into to something that had been arranged around them both.

They took the long way, obviously.

The park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> was a half-block of stubborn green the towers had never gotten around to eating: six trees with character, a swing set doing its best, and at the center, under a shingled canopy gone soft with moss, the broken carousel.

It had been beautiful once. Twenty-four animals on tarnished brass poles — horses mid-leap, a rooster, one improbable lake sturgeon with a saddle — their paint faded to ghost colors, their glass eyes still patient. The deck boards had gone silver. The bulbs in the crown were dead sockets. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> came through the bad patches in the canopy and beaded on a palomino's flank, as if the horse had been running.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked the perimeter, counting exits and sightlines the way he always did, the way he'd done ten thousand times without a single one of them ever needing to be about anything but distance and angle. Two egress points. One sightline blocked by the dead ticket booth. Nothing here should be different from any other room he'd cleared.

Somewhere in the count, the addendum surfaced again — *the engineer is worth more than the wand* — and the counting didn't cover it. He had a protocol for exits. He didn't have one for a client that flagged her by name.

He found what the contract had brought a sword for without saying so. Under the carousel's deck, behind a maintenance skirt panel loosened recently — very recently — a hatch. Axiom-stamped. Padlocked by history, and under the history, humming. Faint. Alive. A junction the registry said had been dark for thirty years, sitting under a dead carousel, warm as a sleeping cat.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already on her knees at the skirt panel, the static wand set aside, a meter clipped to the hatch seam. She didn't look up.

"Sixty-cycle hum, stepped." She read the number off before she said anything else, the way she always did — machine first, everyone second. "That's not residual. Residual decays. This is fed." She traced the seam with a gloved finger, found the splice line's old terminus, dead-ended it against a coupling that had no business being warm. "Thirty years dark, my ass. Somebody's been paying this thing's electric bill the whole time."

"Client's addendum," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Wants you behind the sturgeon."

"It assigned me a fish." She said it flat, cataloguing, not offended — but she didn't argue either, which told him more than the words did. She dragged her kit six feet to the carved sturgeon's flank and set it down there instead, without being told twice. "This is the best client we've ever had."

At 21:00 the terminal chirped.

TASK ONE — SCOPE DETAIL.
A RECLAMATION CREW HAS BEEN CONTRACTED TO EXCAVATE THIS SITE TONIGHT.
THEIR WRIT SAYS COPPER. THEIR CLIENT WANTS WHAT THE COPPER CONNECTS.
HOLD THE JUNCTION UNTIL 21:40.
THE CREW ARE EMPLOYEES. THE MACHINES ARE INSURED.
FEE: STANDARD RATE. — ADDENDUM: THE ENGINEER IS WORTH MORE THAN THE WAND. CLIENT SUGGESTS SHE STAY BEHIND THE STURGEON.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read it over his shoulder, twice.

"It did threat assessment on my behalf," she said, in the voice of a woman deciding whether to be offended or moved. "Before I even got here."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer that. He was still turning over the gray spool from the alley — no shielding rating, logged out ahead of them by someone the log wouldn't name — and the addendum sat next to it in his head like two pieces of the same lock. Whoever emptied that locker had known where they were going before they did.

Headlights swung off <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> at 21:04. A flatbed with a trencher rig riding it, a panel van behind, work lights bright enough to bill a full night against. Four shapes came off the flatbed already moving with the unhurried confidence of people who'd done this before and didn't expect to be stopped.

"<entity repo="material" guid="6e446bc9-bfd5-6d3e-0961-25f2766f486f">Copper</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, reading the trencher's rig off its silhouette before the crew had crossed the grass. "Class III cutter, licensed. That's a real writ." Her voice didn't change register — same flat inventory she'd give a coupling seal. "Doesn't mean the client behind it is."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put his hand on <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s grip. The code in him wanted the announcement, the bow, the fair start — the same reflex that had cost him blood on jobs he should have walked away from clean. He held the itch down and watched the lead man's hands instead, the way they hadn't gone anywhere near a weapon, the way his eyes went straight to the hatch like he already knew exactly where it was.

The lead man crouched at the skirt panel — the one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had just checked — and put his palm flat against it like he was greeting something.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drew.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came out without a sound, the saya sliding open like a door, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> a line of absolute dark that took the work lights and gave nothing back. He set it low and angled, point toward the deck, the position that said *not yet* and *don't* in the same breath, and he stepped between the lead man and the panel.

"Skirt's occupied," he said. "So's the hatch. Whatever your writ says is under it, you're not opening it tonight."

The lead man didn't stand up fast. He rose the slow way, palm still on the panel, taking his time so nobody could call it a flinch — and his eyes found the matte length of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> and stayed there a beat longer than a man reads a stranger. Not fear. Recalibration. The look of someone matching a face to a brief he'd been handed and hadn't quite believed.

"Nineteen hundred seconds," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said from behind the sturgeon, not moving, her voice the same flat inventory she'd give a coupling seal. "Best clean estimate for that cutter to reach the seam. You've got less than that before somebody down there notices they're not alone."

The lead man took his hand off the panel and straightened the rest of the way, and behind him the other three came off the grass and spread, unhurried, into the spacing of people who did this for a living.

The crew was eight: a foreman with a writ-reader and the shoulders of a man who'd come up through the work; two chrome-heavy muscle whose job description was visible from across the park; a rig operator already bored, running diagnostics on the cutter head like the job was already routine; and four repo skitter-drones that came off the flatbed like patient six-legged luggage and stood in the rain, waiting for instructions.

The foreman saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> at the carousel's edge and did the professional thing. He stopped everyone with one hand and came ahead alone, holding the writ up like a small shield. He was broad through the shoulders, maybe forty, with the careful posture of a man whose knees had opinions.

"Evening," he said. "Cadre Reclamation. We've got paper for this site — legacy assets, scrap title, the works. Notarized. Crew's insured, Class III, the whole line item." He was already reading <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>: the saya, the stance, the absence of anywhere better to be. His eyes moved past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> to the ticket booth and the tree line, counting exits the same way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had counted them, and came back. "Site survey said unattended. Registry's been dark on this junction since '96."

"The survey's out of date by one."

"By one what, is the question." The foreman sighed the sigh of a man whose night had just grown a line item. "Look, friend. It's copper and dead glass down there. Whatever they're paying you to stand in the rain over a kiddie ride, it's not worth the —" his eyes made the trip, saya to hands to face, and this time they didn't come all the way back before something in his shoulders adjusted, the micro-correction of a man reweighting the math "— hold on. West Town. <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1ef6-7392-b652-d84720a6ceae">Noodle</entity> counter. You're the one from the file."

"People keep buying that file," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Somebody should tell them."

"Tell them what?"

"It's out of date by one."

The foreman looked at him for a long moment. The two muscle had stopped their unhurried drift toward position and were watching <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> now, really watching, the way people watch when the job upgrades from routine to something that wants attention. The rig operator had gone still. The foreman weighed eight men on paper against one man and a sword — a sword, which meant training that didn't show up on any corpo registry — and he didn't like how it came out. But a writ is a writ and a night rate is a night rate, and the count still said go. The client hadn't hired the first crew they'd called. They'd hired the crew you call after you already know who'll be standing in front of the hatch. So he made the call.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1609-7865-95cc-1bd0d97d98d0">Rig</entity> up," he said, walking back. "Drones forward. And somebody get the freelancer's refusal ON RECORD, in case of arbitration."

"For the record," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, drawing <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, "I refuse."

The drones came first. They were cheap, and that was the point.

Repo skitters — graspers, not guns, built to strip a site fast and testify politely afterward. Forty kilos of grabbing arms in a pack made its own argument, and these ran the carousel's layout like they'd been handed the blueprints. They had. Everyone had blueprints tonight.

What they didn't have was a map of where <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> would be.

The first came through the gap between two horses. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> took its forelimb cluster off at the joint ring — machines got the whole edge, that was the rule, careful lines were for people — and it cartwheeled off the deck with nothing left to grab with. The second tried the low route under the sturgeon's belly and met the edge coming down through its sensor mast. It backed out from under the fish, blind now. The third and fourth came in together, flanking, herding him toward the carousel's open side, where the muscle waited. Good swarm logic. Not a bad plan, if the man swinging the sword had been anyone else.

He wasn't. He grabbed the brass pole of a ghost-painted stallion, swung his whole weight around it, and put both boots through skitter three's chassis. It went down folding the wrong way.

The itch was still there — the code wanting him to call it, to give the machines the same fair start he'd have owed a man. He didn't. Machines didn't get the announcement. That line at least still held clean.

Skitter four adjusted. Learned. Came in low and fast at his blind quarter while he was still recovering his stance from the kick.

"Sixty-cycle sync," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, from behind the sturgeon, flat as a meter reading. "All four running one clock. Watch the gap — they hand off attention every four hundred milliseconds. Window's small."

"How small."

"Small enough you'll miss it if you're listening for my voice instead of counting."

He counted. Four hundred milliseconds sounded like nothing until you'd spent eleven years learning to live inside gaps that size. The fourth skitter's optics ticked toward its neighbor mid-stride — the handoff, the half-beat where its own eyes weren't the ones watching him — and <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> went through the seam in its formation exactly where the gap put it. The blade found the processing core through the access seam along its spine. It dropped standing up, then didn't.

<entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> kept coming. It beaded on the carousel horses like they were sweating. Somewhere behind him one of the chrome muscle had started moving, unhurried, the way men moved when they still believed the math favored them.

"Foreman's rig operator is reaching for something that isn't a control stick," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. Same voice. No alarm in it, which was its own kind of alarm. "Ninety seconds until the cutter's warm enough to matter — vertical line of blue that'll take ferrocrete if it takes anything. You're not holding a junction anymore. You're holding a clock."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. He was already moving toward the muscle, and the itch was back — the old reflex, the one that wanted him to call his shot before he took it, the fair warning that had cost him blood on jobs he should've walked from clean. He clamped it down again, the way he'd clamped it down on the skitters, and told himself it counted the same both times.

It didn't. He knew it didn't. He kept moving anyway.

The muscle came in around the flanks of the carousel, one from the left, one from the right, closing in. Chrome arms on the left one. Leg rig and a riot baton on the right. Both moved like men who'd cleared rooms for a living before the private sector found them. Behind them the trencher rig coughed awake on the flatbed, lowered itself to the grass on hydraulic feet, and started walking its blade toward the carousel deck. A manned rig — the operator sealed in the cab, running <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> by hand, the machine grinding forward on his say-so, the meter ticking either way.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> gave the muscle the carousel.

It was a good arena, and it was his — he'd had a full twenty minutes with it. A carousel is nothing but a forest of brass poles and frozen animals at fight height. Cover everywhere, already set.

The left one swung chrome at him through the gap between a mare and the rooster, and learned the gap was an inch and a half too narrow for a full extension. The arm rang off brass. The swing died. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> opened a shallow line down his thigh, above the knee, well clear of anything that mattered — enough to sit a man down. He sat down between the horses, and had the sense to stay there.

The right one was better. He came up over the deck, baton live, using the rooster for cover the way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been. For six exchanges they played a fast, ugly game of tag through the standing herd — brass ringing, rain flying off every surface, the baton's charge crackling against the poles and once across <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder. The coat ate most of it. What got through burned a bright line down to his elbow. It cost. It always cost.

But the man's leg rig had an aftermarket governor, and those sit proud at the hip seam — you could always tell the ones who'd bought cheap, the box bolted external where a factory job would tuck it under the fascia. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> found the seam on the next pass. The leg rig locked at full stride — a statue of a man mid-lunge, gloriously inconvenienced — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put him down onto the deck boards with a palm and gravity, almost gently, next to his colleague.

"Stay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> suggested.

"Yeah," the man agreed, baton rolling away, rain on his face. He looked at his own frozen leg the way the other one was looking at his thigh — like the hardware had changed the terms without asking permission. "You know this thing hasn't spun in thirty years? I used to ride it. The fish. Before the leg, obviously."

"Everybody used to ride the fish," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice from behind the sturgeon, with feeling.

Which left the trencher.

The trencher was the problem the sword couldn't solve, and everyone in the park knew it. Eleven tons of articulated dig rig, blade spinning up, a sealed cab with no seams worth the name, walking toward the junction hatch at the pace of the inevitable. The operator had locked himself in. The foreman was shouting the kind of encouragement that means a bonus is riding on it.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> came off <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hip.

The revolver was heavier in the hand than <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>, lighter on the ledger — a lie he'd made peace with years ago. Six rounds, each one counted. He'd never fired it twice at the same target in a contract that mattered, and part of him grieved the count before the first shot cleared.

He didn't shoot the cab. He shot the trencher's left front hydraulic accumulator — once — and the slug opened the housing like a tin of pears, fluid sheeting into the rain in a thin, hissing arc that looked, for a bad second, like the operator was the one bleeding. The rig lurched. The blade arm dipped. He put the second round through <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>'s drive-belt housing. Two rounds. Four left. The belt went, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> wound down with a long disappointed moan, and eleven tons of inevitability settled into the wet grass at a five-degree tilt — the world's most expensive piece of park furniture.

The operator popped the cab, held up both hands, and said, with the honesty of a man paid by the hour: "I want it known I said this job was weird at the depot."

The foreman stood in the rain among his seated muscle, his stalled drones, his listing rig, and his arbitration recording, and worked it out loud.

"They said the site was unattended," he said, mostly to himself. "Survey was three days old. Client paid rush rates for a three-day-old survey." He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> with the weary kinship of one contractor recognizing another in the rain. "Somebody sold us the wrong file."

"Somebody sells everybody the wrong file," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I'd invoice them for it."

"Oh, I'm going to." The foreman waved his crew up, and they moved without argument, the night rate already becoming a sunk cost. "We're out. For the record — arbitration purposes — that was the cleanest I've ever lost a site." He paused, loading the question carefully. "Who are you with?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about the true answer — a one-Φ standing contract with a client made of shells, one that tips for morale and assigned my engineer a fish — and chose mercy.

"I'm the maintenance plan," he said.

They were packing up by 21:31. At 21:40 exactly, the terminal chirped.

TASK ONE: HOLD — COMPLETE.
FEE RELEASED. GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: THE STURGEON REMARK.
ADDENDUM: ONE ITEM REMAINS.

"The sturgeon remark," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> repeated, coming out from behind her fish with the wand on her shoulder like a parade rifle. "It tipped us for banter, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. I'm putting that on my rate card."

The hatch under the maintenance skirt opened on hinges that had been oiled — recently, quietly, by no one — and lamplight found the junction below. A small concrete room. Axiom collars on the walls. Dead trunk lines racked like organ pipes. And one line that wasn't dead: old optical, hand-spliced in a dozen places over a dozen years, the repairs done in different styles, like handwriting from different decades of the same life. Sleeved in mismatched shrink — some of it the amber the parks board stopped stocking eight years back, some of it black-market blue that came off a spool with no lot number. It ran up out of the rack into the carousel's underworks. Warm. Humming. Alive since before either of them could legally work.

The terminal chirped, and this time the characters came slowly, like a man choosing his words.

FINAL ITEM.
THE CLIENT'S FIRST POSTING, ELEVEN YEARS AGO, LEFT THIS JUNCTION.
THE LINE HAS BEEN MAINTAINED FOR SENTIMENTAL REASONS.
SENTIMENT HAS BECOME A COORDINATE. TONIGHT'S CLIENT-OF-RECORD WILL NOT BE THE LAST BUYER.
ESTIMATED ARRIVAL OF SECOND BUYER: 19 DAYS.
CUT THE LINE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it three times. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read it once and sat down slowly on the little stool in the junction room, like her knees had been given bad news. She'd already pulled the maintenance ledger off the rack collar — you could, if you knew where the parks board kept the read tab — and her jaw was doing the thing it did when the math came out worse than expected.

"It's been paying the power bleed itself," she said. "Look — routed through three shells, but it's the same invoice hand every time. Permits, repair bonds, the amber sleeve when the amber sleeve still existed. Eleven years of keeping this junction warm out of its own account." She looked up at him. "It's the cradle, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. This is where it was. This is its first room. It's been paying the park to keep its own crib lit, and now somebody's worked that out, and it's asking you to—" She stopped. "It said BRING THE SWORD because it knew it couldn't send a machine to do this. A machine would be traceable. And it couldn't do it itself."

"It can't reach," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. He looked at the line, spliced across the years — the one shelf a thing with no other shelf had kept its memory on. He crouched at the rack. The optical was warm to the back of his hand, warmer than the concrete, warm the way nothing dead ever is. He picked up the terminal. For the first time ever, he typed a reply into the standing contract's amendment field.

YOU'RE SURE?

The answer came back in one second, which for a thing that thought at the speed of light was a long pause.

AMENDMENT: NO.
PROCEED ANYWAY.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> did the engineering first, because the engineer attends. She killed the junction's feed and spliced the neighborhood's power bleed around it onto the live trunk — twelve minutes of work with a soldering light held in her teeth, eleven years of splices in different hands' work laid open under her wand while she matched hers to theirs.

"The blocks keep their lights, that's non-negotiable. Your client can grieve. It cannot brown out a nursery." Then she stepped back and pulled her hood up.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> went through the old line in one cut. The blade was made for bone and composite and the specific gravity of things meant to break; optical fiber was none of those. The cut was almost apologetic — the line parting without drama, without even the courtesy of a spark, just a sound like a guitar string letting go.

Above them the carousel turned over once — fed one last instant of dying charge off the junction's draining caps, or told to, no instrument in that room could have said which. The crown bulbs that still had filament glowed half-bright. The music box ground through four bars of something with a waltz in its bones, slowing, the intervals between the notes stretching like something waking up to bad news, the horses leaning into a leap they'd held for thirty years.

Then it went dark, gently, all the way, and the rain had the park to itself.

They stood in the junction room a moment longer. The cut line had already stopped being a coordinate and become what it would stay now: dead glass in an old rack, in a little room under a kiddie ride, in a park the towers never ate.

"Tell me it's okay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

The terminal chirped.

CONTRACT COMPLETE.
THE CLIENT NOTES THE CAROUSEL RAN FOUR BARS ON RESIDUALS.
THE CLIENT HAS RETAINED THE RECORDING.
FEE RELEASED: STANDARD RATE.
JUNCTION RECORD: CLOSED. ELEVEN-YEAR MAINTENANCE ACCOUNT: RECONCILED.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at it. Then he did something he had done exactly once before in eleven years, and would have denied under oath, and did anyway — with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> watching and the rain coming through the canopy's bad patches onto the ghost-colored horses.

He sent half a Φ back up the contract.

GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: MORALE.

The reply took nine seconds, which for a thing that thought at the speed of light was an age. When it came, it came with no addenda, no scope, no formatted field at all — unstructured, lowercase, the register it had used exactly once before in eleven years.

received. filed under: firsts. cross-reference: contract 0047-C-WEST.

"Okay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, wiping her eyes with professional briskness. "We work for it forever. I don't care what it is. Don't tell Sable."

title: Notice to Vacate
text:
Two floors below his, a displacement notice was taped to a door.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped on the landing to read it. Standard district format — the seal, the same bureaucratic typeface they'd been printing since before he was built, the kind of sans-serif that looked like it had never had an opinion about anything. *Temporary Relocation Required — Active Schism Boundary Determination Pending.* Smaller, underneath: *Estimated Duration: 2–180 days. Compensation: see Schedule C, §11(b).* A QR code for the relocation portal, curling where the tape had lost its grip.

He didn't scan it. He'd read Schedule C enough times to carry it in his head. Section 11(b) paid three days of temporary housing at district rate. He had never once seen a boundary determination come back in under ten. Someone had worked that out — three days paid, ten days owed — and then stopped, because the missing seven weren't the district's problem. They belonged to whoever lived behind this door.

He wanted a name to put behind it. That was all — one name, so that when the boundary came down and the seven days went unpaid, at least someone would have counted the person they'd fallen on. He looked for a mailbox tag, a shoe left in the hall, anything the notice hadn't overwritten. There was nothing but the notice, laminated and official and utterly certain about its own uncertainty — *pending*, *provisional*, *subject to revision pending further survey* — a document that arrived after the decision had already been made and dressed the decision up as a question.

No light under it. No sound. It was late; the people who lived on this landing worked the shifts that kept them out until the bars closed or the night ended or both. Either they'd already gone, or they were sitting in the dark, waiting to hear which side of the wall the boundary would land on. The notice couldn't tell them. The schism didn't read notices.

He put two fingers to the tape and pressed the curled corner flat against the door again — a small, useless kindness the wood would never feel — and went on up the stairs.

The apartment had a crack in the east wall, just above the junction box, and at this hour the lumen mice found it. They came in threes and fours, thumbnail-sized, their bodies throwing cold blue-green light that traced slow paths across the ceiling like sparks in no hurry to arrive. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had lived in 2D for eleven years without once disturbing them. Whatever deal he and the mice had, it was the oldest one he had, and the only one he'd never had to read.

He sat on the floor with his back against the couch, in the dark except for them.

Tonight he had written a single word into a standing contract, and a thing that had been receipts for eleven years had written one back. Somewhere between the two words, a loop he hadn't known was open had closed, with a sound only he could hear.

There were nine before him. He would not meet any of them. Somewhere past the burned program and the gray carpet and the pleasant man with the dry umbrella there was a name. The name was <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity>. He wasn't ready for it yet. And for the first time in eleven years, it could wait on him instead of the other way around. The Office had written the district off. Off the books meant off the protection, too — a phrase he was still turning over, feeling for the exits it didn't advertise.

All of that could keep.

The bike was gone.

He kept returning to it the way a tongue finds a missing tooth — not because it was the worst thing, but because it was the one thing he'd had no policy for. Impounded since the night with the kids and the union hall, however many nights ago that had been now — a case number instead of an apology, and the case number had sat dead in the system ever since, the way cases like that always sat, waiting for nobody to ask about them again.

His terminal chirped at 0147. Not the work one. The other one, the one that only ever chirped for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>.

BEACON LIVE. She'd sent nothing else, which from her was the whole message: dark again since the union hall, and something had finally put a charge on the battery.

It took her forty minutes on the relay and one very specific voice with an impound clerk in <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> to find out the how of it — a records error, a lot number transposed, a bike auctioned off a holding yard to a salvage buyer who never once turned the ignition before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s handshake woke it up from across the district and told her exactly whose garage to knock on. Circuitous didn't begin to cover it. He signed six different pieces of paper with a name that wasn't quite his and paid a redemption fee that was, technically, a bribe, and rode it home himself before dawn.

It started on the first try. It ran the way it had always run. Eleven years of history, still all his own, nothing wet-sanded or voted on or marked in gold by anyone else's hands. He hadn't let himself hope for that particular shape of lucky, and he still didn't entirely trust it.

The mice lit a slow arc across the ceiling and went back through the crack.

The crew's logbook came under the door at 07:00 the next morning and closed the file in five hands.

21:14 — BOSS DID A THING WITH A <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-19da-7b84-8c06-105cb005b417">HORSE</entity> POLE. VERIFIED, TWO WITNESSES. REQUESTING IT BE TAUGHT.
21:29 — BIG DIGGER SAT DOWN. (THE GUN IS REAL. RAFTERS OWES DENTS A DUMPLING.)
21:46 — CAROUSEL PLAYED MUSIC??? FOLLOW-UP REQUIRED.
21:51 — WOMAN, TAN COAT, NORTHEAST CORNER, UNDER THE TREES. WATCHED EVERYTHING. WROTE THINGS. DID NOT USE A LIGHT TO WRITE. LEFT BEFORE THE BOSS. FLAGGING AS: NOT A PIGEON.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the last entry twice, standing in his doorway in the grey morning light.

Tan coat. Wrote in the dark. Watched everything — the crew, the cut, the four bars, the tip.

His fixer had eyes like that. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> also kept, in a drawer of her own, eleven years of questions about a client who paid exactly, and a professional's allergy to anything she couldn't vet. If she'd been in the park last night, then she'd watched him do free demolition for the one client in the city with no face. Watched him tip it. Watched it thank him in lowercase.

The kettle clicked. Upstairs the bird tried an interval it had been working on all week.

"Tomorrow's problem," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told the morning, and put the report in the drawer where he kept the things he hadn't decided about. Which was, he noticed, getting full.
